---
title: "Final Project"
---

Each student writes a reproducible statistical analysis of a public health
dataset: a Quarto report in a GitHub repository, a 5-minute video walkthrough,
and an AI-use appendix. The project is worth **30% of your course grade** and is
scored out of **100 points**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Due 11:59 PM ET, Wednesday December 16, 2026

Your **last push** to your project repository before the deadline is graded.
No late submissions are accepted. If you have an approved accommodation, contact
the instructor well before the deadline.
:::

## Getting started

1. **Accept the assignment:**
   [Final Project on Classroom 50](https://classroom50.org/gph-2182/gph-gu-2182-fall-2026/assignments/final-project/accept).
   This creates your private repository from the starter template.
2. **Open it in RStudio.** In the Console:

   ```r
   source("https://gph-2182.github.io/gph2182.R")
   gph_project()
   ```

3. **Pick your dataset** from the menu below and submit a
   [dataset proposal](#dataset-proposal-5-points) in `proposal.md` by
   **Wednesday, November 18**.
4. **Once it is approved, write `report.qmd`**, render it to `report.html`, and push often with
   `gph_submit()` (or commit and push from the Git tab). Every push is a backup.

The starter repository contains:

| File | What it is |
|:---|:---|
| `proposal.md` | Your dataset proposal (5 points). |
| `report.qmd` | Your report. Its section headings match the rubric below. |
| `data/` | The COVID-19 data files (Option A) and a data dictionary for every option. Put your own data files here too. |
| `README.md` | Your name, NetID, video link, and integrity statement. |

## Choose a dataset

Pick **one** primary dataset. You may bring in additional public data to enrich
it (for example, state populations to turn case counts into rates); cite every
source you use.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### A. US COVID-19 (NYT)

Daily **cumulative** COVID-19 cases and deaths for the United States and each
state, January 2020 to March 23, 2023, from
[The New York Times](https://github.com/nytimes/covid-19-data), free for
non-commercial use with credit to The New York Times.

* Files (already in your `data/` folder): `us.csv` (one row per day for the
  whole country) and `us-states.csv` (one row per state or territory per day).
* Columns: `date`, `state`, `fips`, `cases`, `deaths`.
* Watch out: the counts are **cumulative**, so daily new cases are differences
  between consecutive days; reporting backlogs make some differences negative.
* Use the copies in `data/`, not the live GitHub files, so everyone works from
  the same snapshot.

### B. NHANES

A survey-based sample of **10,000 US residents** from the 2009 to 2012 National
Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, with about 75 variables on demographics,
body measurements, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, sleep, physical
activity, smoking, and alcohol.

* Load it with `library(NHANES)` and the data frame `NHANES` (install the
  package once with `install.packages("NHANES")` in the Console, never inside
  your report).
* Documentation: `?NHANES` in R.
* Watch out: many variables apply only to some ages (for example adults 20+),
  so missing values are common and often meaningful. The package version has
  been resampled for teaching, so describe results as patterns in this sample,
  not official US estimates.

### C. Gapminder (`gm`)

The `gm` data from the course package `r02pro`: country-year records of life
expectancy, child mortality, income, BMI, smoking, cancer incidence, health
spending, and more.

* Load it with `library(r02pro)`; documentation is `?gm`.
* Watch out: units vary by column (check `?gm` before converting anything),
  and coverage differs a lot across variables and years.
* You have used `gm` all semester, so the bar for a fresh question is higher:
  combine variables in a way we did not in class, or join `gm` with another
  public dataset.

### D. Your own dataset

Any **public** public-health dataset you can legally share in your repository,
for example from [NYC Open Data](https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/),
[CDC data](https://data.cdc.gov/), the
[WHO Global Health Observatory](https://www.who.int/data/gho), or
[Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/).

* Describe it in your [dataset proposal](#dataset-proposal-5-points), like
  every other option: the source link, its license or terms of use, and the
  exact column names you plan to use.
* Files must be under 50 MB each so they fit in your repository.
* No individual-level data that is not already public and de-identified.

:::

## Dataset proposal (5 points)

Every student submits a short proposal, whichever option they choose. It is
graded, and you write your report only on an **approved** dataset and question.

1. Open your project (`gph_project()`) and fill in every line of
   **`proposal.md`**: your option, the dataset and its source link, a
   one-sentence research question, the 3 to 6 exact column names you plan to
   use, and your planned analysis. Tick the three data-checklist boxes.
2. Run **`gph_submit()`**, the same way you push homework.
3. Check the decision with **`gph_proposal()`** in the Console. It says
   **approved**, **needs changes** (with comments), or **waiting for review**.
   The decision also appears in your repository as `proposal-review.md` and
   as a comment on your repository's Feedback pull request, and GitHub e-mails
   you when it arrives.
4. If it needs changes, edit `proposal.md` and run `gph_submit()` again. You
   can revise as many times as you need; revising costs nothing.

| Proposal points | When |
|:---|:---|
| 5 | First version pushed by **Wed Nov 18, 11:59 PM ET**, and the approved version pushed by **Wed Nov 25, 11:59 PM ET**. |
| 2.5 | Approved, but the first version came after Nov 18 or the approved version after Nov 25. |
| 0 | Never approved. |

A good proposal names a question one dataset can answer, lists real column
names (for example `SleepHrsNight` and `BMI` in NHANES, or `cases` in the COVID
files), and says what you will compute from them (daily new cases from the
cumulative counts is fine). Option C proposals must go beyond what we did with
`gm` in class.

## What your report must contain

Your report tells a **story** with the data. Do not just list statistics; build
a coherent argument that answers a question you care about, in a way your
classmates probably will not.

1. **Introduction.** The question, why a public health reader should care, the
   data and methods you use, and what the reader will learn.
2. **Packages and data preparation.** Load every package in one chunk at the
   top and say what each is for. Cite and link the data source; describe how
   it was collected and any quirks (missing values, units, cumulative counts).
   Explain each cleaning step and why you did it. Show the final data
   compactly (never print hundreds of rows) and summarize the variables you
   use in a table or a short paragraph with inline R.
3. **Exploratory analysis.** Reveal something that is not obvious from the raw
   data: create new variables, summarize by groups, reshape, or join tables.
   Include **at least three `ggplot2` figures**, each making one clear point
   with informative titles, axis labels, and units, and **at least one
   well-formatted table**. Explain every figure and table in words, quoting
   key numbers with inline R.
4. **Going further: functions plus simulation or modeling.** Write **at least
   one custom function** with input checks that you use more than once, and
   use **either** a simulation (for example a bootstrap interval or a
   permutation test, Week 10) **or** a regression model with `lm()`/`glm()`
   (Week 11). Interpret the result in plain language and state its
   limitations.
5. **Summary.** The question, how you answered it, the main findings, what
   they mean for the reader, the limitations, and what you would do next.
6. **AI-use appendix** (the last section of the report; see below).

Every number in your text comes from R (inline code), never typed by hand.
A rendered report of roughly 2,000 to 3,500 words, not counting code, is
typical; clarity matters more than length.

### The video walkthrough

A screen recording of **at most 5 minutes** (Zoom, Loom, NYU Stream, or
similar) in which you present your question, your data, two or three key
figures, your main finding, and one thing you learned or would do differently.
Show your face or not, your choice. Put the link in your `README.md` and make
sure anyone at NYU with the link can watch it.

### The AI-use appendix

AI assistants are permitted for this project (see the
[AI policy](ai-policy.qmd)), and every use must be disclosed. For each
substantive use, record:

* the tool, and what you asked (a summary or the prompt itself);
* what it produced and which parts you kept, changed, or rejected;
* **how you verified** the result (checked it against a known value, read the
  documentation, compared with a second method, tested edge cases).

Include at least one example where the AI was wrong, incomplete, or needed
changes, and what you learned from it. If you did not use AI at all, say so,
and instead document how you verified two of your key results. Copying output
you cannot explain is not allowed, whether it came from an AI or a person.

## Grading rubric (100 points)

| Component | Criteria | Points |
|:---|:---|---:|
| **Dataset proposal** | Submitted in `proposal.md` by Nov 18 and approved by Nov 25 (see [Dataset proposal](#dataset-proposal-5-points)). | 5 |
| **Introduction** | Clear question and motivation; data and approach outlined; what the reader gains. | 5 |
| **Packages & data preparation** | Packages loaded upfront and explained; source cited and described; cleaning steps logical and justified; final data shown compactly; variable summary. | 15 |
| **Exploratory analysis** | Goes beyond the raw data (new variables, groups, reshaping, joins); at least three purposeful, well-labeled figures and one well-built table; insights explained with numbers from inline R. | 15 |
| **Functions + simulation or modeling** | A reusable, checked custom function used more than once; a simulation or regression that fits the question, correctly interpreted, with limitations. | 10 |
| **Summary** | Question, approach, findings, implications, limitations, next steps. | 5 |
| **Reproducibility & code quality** | Renders from a fresh clone with no errors; relative paths only (no `setwd()`, no `install.packages()` in the report); seed set once for any randomness; readable, commented, well-organized code; `report.html` matches `report.qmd`. | 15 |
| **Video walkthrough** | At most 5 minutes; covers question, data, key figures, main finding, and a reflection; clear and audible; link works. | 15 |
| **AI-use appendix** | Every use disclosed with what was asked and kept; concrete verification for each; at least one documented AI error or fix, with reflection (or, if no AI used, two documented verifications). | 15 |
| | **Total** | **100** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,68,10]"}

The rubric was adapted from the
[UC Business Analytics R Programming Guide](http://uc-r.github.io/data_wrangling/final-project)
final project rubric.
